prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins

statement.case_for: Three members placed B011 first and five placed it in their top three, and I now agree that it is the strongest case on the shortlist. The principle is simple and quantitative: a bifunctional molecule forms a ternary complex that turns binding into elimination of the target, and the cooperativity of that complex gives a design rule that can be tested. It opens previously unforeseen opportunities because proteins once called undruggable become accessible. The 2001 Sakamoto, Kim, Crews and Deshaies work gave the concept, and Ciulli's VHL ligands and structural analysis of ternary complexes turned it into rational chemistry. Independent reproduction is wide and degraders are in late-stage trials. A Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli citation is easy to explain to a broad audience.
statement.case_against: No degrader is yet a broadly approved drug, so the clinical proof that usually follows a prize of this kind is still pending, and the prize could look early. Limiting it to three names leaves out Sakamoto and Kim from the founding paper and sets aside the molecular-glue strand of Handa, Ito and Gray, which is a distinct lineage with its own claim. Any citation that says protein degradation will be read as covering both strands, so the omission has to be defended openly.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B011 first but proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa, because Handa's identification of cereblon underpins molecular glues and explains thalidomide-class drugs.
responses.response: I respect the mechanistic weight of the cereblon discovery, but I disagree on the credit. It is a separate discovery about the target of thalidomide. The PROTAC concept and the structure-guided design rules, where Ciulli matters more, are what make degradation a general chemical capability. I would keep Handa and Ito for a possible later recognition of molecular glues, unless Andrei can show that the glue strand cannot be separated from the citation.

responses.point: Aqvist calls targeted degradation a new pharmacological principle that removes the target instead of blocking it, with real consequences already, and notes it may still be slightly early.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and with his standard of a simple concept with real consequences. On timing I would press further. Twenty years since the first PROTAC and many independent groups is a strong record, but without approved drugs the citation should stay on the chemical principle and not claim therapeutic success. Johan, do you think the committee would accept that wording as defensible?

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range electron transfer through proteins (B058, Gray and Winkler) first, because it states a biological mechanism in physical terms, with tunnelling rates set by distance and medium, and it is mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I find this the best physical-chemistry case other than B011, and the science is fully mature. My reservation is scope. Marcus theory, Hopfield, and Moser and Dutton already carry much of the conceptual credit, and I would need Peter to define what exactly Gray and Winkler discovered that others did not. If that is settled, B058 deserves a second look next to B011. At present I do not think it displaces B011, which opens a new capability.

responses.point: Sparr ranks phase separation (B035) first as a general physical-chemical organizing principle of the cell, but admits that its biological generality and disease relevance are still debated and that the three-person limit leaves credit unresolved.
responses.response: The thermodynamic framework is attractive to a physicist and I take the concept seriously. Her own caveats are the problem. If generality is still debated, the committee cannot write a citation that claims more than the evidence supports, and Pappu and Mittag are left out of any three-name split. I would prefer to wait than to cut credit that may later look wrong.

responses.point: Zou ranks dye-sensitized solar cells (B005, Grätzel and O'Regan) first, as a clear, original structure-determines-function principle with more than thirty years of confirmation and adoption.
responses.response: I agree, and I ranked B005 second for the same reasons. The attribution is clean and the maturity beyond doubt. My difference with Xiaodong is about generative capability today: efficiencies have plateaued and commercial use is modest, though it opened perovskite photovoltaics. I keep it as my first alternative, and if B011 stalls on attribution I would be content with B005.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree to leave Sakamoto, Kim, Handa, Ito and Gray out of the citation and defend that.
Whether clinical validation of degraders is mature enough or whether a prize should wait for an approved drug.
Whether B058 (Gray, Winkler) has a distinct enough discovery claim relative to Marcus, Hopfield, and Moser and Dutton.
I have not verified the living status of some credited individuals across ballots.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I share a Lund affiliation with Somfai and Sparr, but none of the shortlisted candidates is connected to Lund University or to my nanophysics research as far as the profile shows. B017 (nanopores) is near my field of nanofabricated devices, so I treat my own opening preference for it with caution and rank it only as an alternative.
